subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Congenital penile abnormalities; descent of testes and ovaries
vignette: A newborn boy is noted to have the urethral meatus located on the ventral (underside) of the penis, proximal to the tip of the glans. There is no dorsal displacement.
question: Which of the following best describes this congenital anomaly?

options.text: Hypospadias due to failure of the urethral folds to fuse
Epispadias due to faulty positioning of the genital tubercle
Hypospadias due to faulty positioning of the genital tubercle
Epispadias due to failure of the urethral folds to fuse
A normal variant of meatal position requiring no concern

explanation_correct: Hypospadias is an abnormal opening of the penile urethra on the ventral (under) surface of the penis, caused by failure of the urethral folds to fuse. It is more common than epispadias and can be associated with inguinal hernia, cryptorchidism, and chordee; it can also be seen in 5-alpha-reductase deficiency. Epispadias, by contrast, places the meatus on the dorsal surface.

explanation_incorrect.B: Epispadias places the meatus on the dorsal (top) surface and results from faulty positioning of the genital tubercle, not a ventral location from failed fold fusion.
explanation_incorrect.C: Faulty positioning of the genital tubercle causes epispadias, not hypospadias; hypospadias results from failed urethral fold fusion.
explanation_incorrect.D: Failure of urethral folds to fuse causes hypospadias with a ventral meatus, not epispadias.
explanation_incorrect.E: A ventrally displaced meatus is hypospadias, a congenital anomaly that may need surgical repair and is associated with other anomalies.

educationalObjective: Hypospadias is a ventral urethral meatus from failure of urethral fold fusion; epispadias is dorsal from faulty genital tubercle positioning.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Congenital penile abnormalities; descent of testes and ovaries
vignette: A newborn is found to have a urethral opening on the dorsal surface of the penis. Further examination reveals an open bladder plate on the anterior abdominal wall.
question: Which condition is classically associated with this dorsal penile urethral defect?
explanation_correct: Epispadias is an abnormal urethral opening on the dorsal (top) surface of the penis caused by faulty positioning of the genital tubercle. It is classically associated with exstrophy of the bladder, as seen here with the exposed bladder plate on the abdominal wall. In contrast, hypospadias is a ventral opening from failed urethral fold fusion and is associated with inguinal hernia, cryptorchidism, chordee, and 5-alpha-reductase deficiency.

explanation_incorrect.A: Inguinal hernia is associated with hypospadias, not with the dorsal defect of epispadias.
explanation_incorrect.B: Cryptorchidism is associated with hypospadias, not epispadias.
explanation_incorrect.D: Imperforate anus is not a classic association of epispadias or bladder exstrophy.
explanation_incorrect.E: 5-alpha-reductase deficiency is associated with hypospadias and atypical genitalia, not epispadias with bladder exstrophy.

educationalObjective: Epispadias is a dorsal meatus from faulty genital tubercle positioning and is associated with bladder exstrophy.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Congenital penile abnormalities; descent of testes and ovaries
vignette: A 2-year-old boy with hypospadias is being evaluated for associated congenital anomalies. His pediatrician reviews the known associations of this condition.
question: Which of the following is a recognized association of hypospadias?

options.text: Chordee (downward or upward curvature of the penis)

explanation_correct: Hypospadias is associated with inguinal hernia, cryptorchidism (undescended testis), and chordee (abnormal downward or upward bending of the penis). It can also be seen in 5-alpha-reductase deficiency. Bladder exstrophy is associated with epispadias, not hypospadias. Recognition of chordee is important because it affects surgical repair.

explanation_incorrect.A: Bladder exstrophy is associated with epispadias, the dorsal defect, not hypospadias.
explanation_incorrect.C: Patent ductus arteriosus is a cardiac defect with no specific association with hypospadias.
explanation_incorrect.D: Cleft palate is an orofacial defect and is not an association of hypospadias.
explanation_incorrect.E: Achondroplasia is a skeletal dysplasia and is not related to penile development.

educationalObjective: Hypospadias is associated with chordee, cryptorchidism, inguinal hernia, and 5-alpha-reductase deficiency.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Congenital penile abnormalities; descent of testes and ovaries
vignette: A neonatologist examines a newborn boy with a painless scrotal swelling that transilluminates. It is due to persistence of the embryonic peritoneal evagination that normally closes before birth.
question: Persistence of which embryonic structure most directly causes this scrotal collection (hydrocele)?
explanation_correct: The processus vaginalis is an evagination of peritoneum that accompanies the descending testis and normally forms the tunica vaginalis. When it remains patent, peritoneal fluid can accumulate around the testis, producing a hydrocele, a painless transilluminating scrotal swelling. The gubernaculum anchors the testis within the scrotum (its female remnants are the ovarian ligament and round ligament of the uterus). The allantois and vitelline duct are unrelated umbilical structures.

explanation_incorrect.A: The gubernaculum anchors the testes in the scrotum; its female remnants are the ovarian and round ligaments, and it does not form the tunica vaginalis.
explanation_incorrect.B: The allantois contributes to the urachus and umbilical vessels; it is not involved in scrotal swelling.
explanation_incorrect.C: The vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct connects the yolk sac to the midgut; its remnants cause Meckel diverticulum, not hydrocele.
explanation_incorrect.E: The mesonephric (Wolffian) duct forms male internal genitalia (SEED); it does not give rise to the tunica vaginalis.

educationalObjective: A persistent patent processus vaginalis causes hydrocele; normally it forms the tunica vaginalis, while the gubernaculum anchors the testis.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Congenital penile abnormalities; descent of testes and ovaries
vignette: A medical student reviews the venous drainage of the gonads. She notes that the left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein at a 90-degree angle, while the right gonadal vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava. She is asked about the clinical implication of this asymmetry.
question: Which of the following correctly states gonadal venous drainage and its clinical consequence?

options.text: Both gonadal veins drain directly into the IVC, so varicoceles are equally common bilaterally
Right gonad drains via the right renal vein; left gonad drains directly into the IVC, making right varicocele more common
Left gonad drains into the inferior mesenteric vein, predisposing to left renal vein thrombosis
Both gonadal veins drain into the renal veins, and varicoceles are more common on the right
Right gonad drains directly to the IVC; left gonad drains via the left renal vein to the IVC, making left varicocele more common

explanation_correct: The right ovary/testis drains via the right gonadal vein directly into the IVC, while the left ovary/testis drains via the left gonadal vein into the left renal vein (and then the IVC), taking the longer route. The left gonadal vein enters the left renal vein at a 90-degree angle, making flow less laminar and raising left venous pressure; this is why varicocele is more common on the left.

explanation_incorrect.A: The left gonadal vein does not drain directly into the IVC; it drains into the left renal vein, and varicoceles are not equally common.
explanation_incorrect.B: The drainage is reversed: the right gonad drains directly to the IVC and the left via the left renal vein, and varicocele is more common on the left, not the right.
explanation_incorrect.C: The gonadal veins do not drain into the inferior mesenteric vein; the left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein.
explanation_incorrect.D: The right gonadal vein does not drain into a renal vein (it goes directly to the IVC), and varicoceles are more common on the left.

educationalObjective: Right gonad drains directly to IVC; left gonad drains via the left renal vein to the IVC; the left route's 90-degree angle explains higher left varicocele frequency.
